 Dengue fever and influenza A are on the rise: Many severe cases are being admitted to emergency rooms.
 TPO - Hospitals in Hanoi are receiving and treating many patients with dengue fever and influenza A, including cases with severe symptoms and potential complications. Notably, dengue fever can become severe even when the patient's fever begins to subside; while influenza A is particularly dangerous for the elderly, those with underlying health conditions, and those with weakened immune systems.
 Báo Tiền Phong • 11/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 The National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is currently treating two female patients, aged 23 and 53, with severe dengue fever. Both have severely low platelet counts, elevated liver enzymes of nearly 2,000 U/L, along with coagulation disorders and signs of organ damage. 
 Patient BH (53 years old, Hai Phong ), previously healthy and with no history of dengue fever, experienced a continuous high fever for about 5 days before hospitalization, sometimes reaching 39-40 degrees Celsius. The patient also experienced general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain. Despite self-medicating with paracetamol at home, the condition did not improve. 
 Patients with severe dengue fever are cared for at the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Upon arrival at the medical facility, the patient was diagnosed with Dengue virus infection, their platelet count rapidly decreased from 38 to 21 G/L, and liver enzymes were elevated, so they were transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases.
 Here, the patient still had a high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) appeared under the skin at the injection site. The patient was diagnosed with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever with liver damage, requiring close monitoring for the risk of bleeding and circulatory disorders.
 The second case involves patient PL (23 years old, Hanoi ), who was previously healthy. Approximately 7 days before being transferred to the hospital, the patient experienced intermittent high fever, sometimes reaching 39 degrees Celsius, accompanied by chills, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and loose stools. Notably, ultrasound revealed fluid in the abdominal cavity and both pleural spaces.
 This could be a sign of plasma leakage, a key mechanism in severe dengue fever, which can lead to decreased circulating volume, hemodynamic instability, and shock if not treated promptly.
 Upon arrival at the hospital, the patient still had a fever, was very tired, had petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin, and experienced pain in the liver area. Doctors assessed this as a severe case of dengue fever with serious liver damage, requiring intensive treatment.
 According to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the unit is currently treating 16 patients with dengue fever, including some cases with severe symptoms.
 According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can occur at all ages, including those who were previously completely healthy.
 According to Dr. Phuc, the severity of the disease cannot be assessed solely based on platelet count. Doctors need to evaluate the overall clinical condition, signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and signs of organ damage.
 You may also like "In these two cases, in addition to a sharp drop in platelets, the patients also had very high liver enzymes, blood clotting disorders, and other warning signs. These abnormalities indicate that the disease has progressed seriously and requires close monitoring to detect and treat complications promptly," Dr. Phuc said. 
 Isolation area for patients with infectious diseases at Thanh Nhan Hospital. Doctors advise patients to seek medical attention immediately if they experience symptoms such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy, restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue. Patients should not increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a doctor's prescription due to the risk of increased bleeding.
 Influenza A cases are on the rise, and elderly patients require oxygen therapy.
 Meanwhile, at the Infectious Diseases Unit, Occupational Diseases Department, Thanh Nhan Hospital, there are currently about 60 patients under treatment, of which about 50 are infected with influenza A. The majority of hospitalized influenza patients are elderly and have multiple underlying health conditions. The disease is also found in immunocompromised individuals, including cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy and radiotherapy. 
 Patients with influenza A are being treated at Thanh Nhan Hospital. After 6 days of hospitalization for influenza A treatment, Ms. Vu Thi Toan (born in 1951, residing in Kim Hoa Street, Hanoi) still requires oxygen. Dr. Nguyen Thu Huong, Head of the Occupational Diseases Department, Musculoskeletal Unit, and Head of the Infectious Diseases Unit, stated that although the influenza A test was negative, the patient is not yet eligible for discharge due to pneumonia and respiratory failure, and the prognosis remains unfavorable.
 Notably, the patient had multiple underlying conditions including hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, and adrenal insufficiency due to medication abuse during treatment.
 According to Doctor Huong, this year the number of influenza A cases has increased rapidly, lasting for more than a month and a half and showing no signs of slowing down. The changing weather , especially during the winter and spring, creates favorable conditions for pathogens to develop.
 The continuously increasing number of patients forced the unit to place extra beds in the aisles. At times, the number of beds in the rooms was insufficient, and the hospital had to arrange additional beds outside. The unit also increased the number of doctors and considered discharging some patients earlier to make room for more severe cases, while still ensuring safe treatment.
 Given the increasing number of cases of influenza A, doctors advise that people experiencing symptoms such as cough, fever, shortness of breath, sneezing, and runny nose should seek medical attention for examination and diagnosis. In particular, individuals with underlying conditions such as cardiovascular disease, hypertension, COPD, asthma, cancer, or immunodeficiency should seek medical attention early to minimize the risk of complications.

 Along with influenza A, the number of dengue fever patients at Thanh Nhan Hospital has also increased compared to the same period last year. To reduce the burden, the Infectious Disease Unit prioritizes admitting approximately 4-5 severe dengue fever patients each day. Mild and moderate cases are treated in other specialties; in case of severe complications, doctors will consult and intervene promptly.
 Mr. NVK (from Bach Mai ward) said that before being hospitalized, he experienced headaches, a fever of 38-39 degrees Celsius, accompanied by dizziness and lightheadedness. After two days at home, he felt faint, fainted, and was taken to the hospital about 15 minutes later.
 This is the third time he has contracted dengue fever. Previous times he also had to be hospitalized, but this time he feels the illness is more severe, with a more prolonged headache. "In previous instances, the headache subsided after the fever went down, but it hasn't this time," Mr. K shared.
 Dr. Phuc emphasized that patients and their families should not assess the severity of the illness based solely on body temperature. A reduction in fever does not necessarily mean the illness has passed the critical stage.
 Attending scheduled follow-up appointments, undergoing prescribed tests, and closely monitoring the patient during the 3rd to 7th day are crucial for early detection of the risk of worsening condition. Patients should not be complacent when their fever subsides or symptoms seem to improve, as this could be the time when the disease enters a dangerous stage.
